## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
### At 4:17

Every afternoon at 4:17, my shadow left me.

There was no drama in it. It simply stopped obeying. If I lifted my cup, my shadow remained beside the chair. If I crossed the room, it stayed at the window, a dark comma on the floor. At 4:27 it returned. Sometimes it brought sand. Sometimes it smelled of rain, though my windows faced a brick wall and the weather had been dry for weeks.

I tried all the usual remedies. I changed the lightbulbs. I moved the furniture. A doctor shone a light into my eyes and asked whether I had been sleeping.

“Mostly,” I said.

She told me to drink less coffee. This seemed unlikely to help, but I did it anyway, because instructions are comforting even when they are wrong.

One Tuesday, I decided to follow it. At 4:16 I put on my shoes, as if footwear might matter. At 4:17 my shadow slid beneath the door. I reached for the handle, but the door opened before I touched it.

On the other side was Mara’s old street.

The bakery that had closed was open. The sycamore outside her building, cut down after a storm, was casting a green net over the pavement. Everything looked slightly worn, as if the street had been living without me.

My shadow waited at the blue door. I followed it upstairs.

Mara stood at the kitchen sink, eleven years older. I knew because eleven was the number I had been avoiding. An older version of me was kneeling beside a broken drawer, trying to repair it with a spoon.

There were two coats on one hook. A brown dog slept on a pile of laundry. Someone had drawn a yellow sun on the refrigerator and given it, for reasons I could not discover, a moustache.

“Leave it,” Mara said. “It’s happier as a shelf.”

He answered with something rude and affectionate. She threw a dish towel at him. The dog did not wake.

Nothing glowed. Nobody was wise. The tap dripped. Mara’s hair was coming loose. I wanted that life so violently that I had to sit down on the floor.

I had imagined happiness as an arrival: a gate, a clear note, a door closing behind you with the past safely outside. This was not that. It was a broken drawer and two people who had learned where to put their tenderness so the other would find it.

Then I noticed the other man’s shadow.

It was not beneath him. It was flattened against the window, though he was kneeling in the light. Beyond it, faint as a reflection in dark glass, was my kitchen: one cup, one chair, the patient brick wall.

He looked up. Not at me—I do not think he could see me—but toward the room I had left. His face held no regret I could name. Only attention. Only the small human ache of a closed door.

Mara asked whether he was going to fix the drawer or adopt it.

He turned back to her, laughing, and at 4:27 the room let me go.

I expected wisdom to feel larger. Instead, for several days, I simply felt ordinary. Every life, it seemed, cast a shadow into some other life. This did not make mine easier. It made it mine, which was not the same thing.

I repaired my own drawer with a screwdriver. I bought a plant and overwatered it. Some evenings I thought of Mara. Some evenings I didn’t, and then felt guilty for not thinking of her, which is one of memory’s little traps.

My shadow still leaves at 4:17. I no longer follow. Everyone should have somewhere to go.

Sometimes it returns with sand on the floor or the ghost of rain. Sometimes there is nothing at all. Yesterday it came back smelling of coffee. I made two cups out of habit, then drank them both while standing at the window.

Outside, the brick wall was turning gold. Somewhere, perhaps, a drawer was being repaired with a spoon. Somewhere, it was holding.

Here, the light moved slowly across the floor. For once, I did not mistake it for something leaving.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION. A polished, lightly surreal short story uses the narrator’s departing shadow to explore a life not lived.

## Grounded reading
The voice is dryly observant and tender, finding the uncanny in ordinary details: a shadow that smells of rain, a doctor’s practical advice, a drawer repaired with a spoon. The story gives real weight to the narrator’s longing for Mara’s imagined life, then turns gently away from the fantasy of a perfect alternate future toward the imperfect life at hand. Its invitation is not to stop wondering, but to let wonder coexist with attention to what remains.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds counterfactual longing, memory, and the small acts through which tenderness takes shape: a dish towel thrown, a drawer left as a shelf, two cups of coffee. Its recurring images of shadows, doors, and light make the alternate life feel close without treating it as a destination the narrator ought to claim.

## Evidence line
> This seemed unlikely to help, but I did it anyway, because instructions are comforting even when they are wrong.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the coherent, distinctive use of ordinary objects to carry restrained emotional weight makes this a revealing sample.
